web_title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Business Cycles
book_title: Chapter 1: From Paper Airline to ASEAN Freighter — How Afcom Got Here
question: How did a 2013 Chennai freight-charter startup evolve into a scheduled international cargo airline, and what capital cycles shaped its balance sheet?

epigraph.quote: Aviation is the art of turning fixed lease obligations into variable route profits before the fuel bill arrives.
epigraph.author: Institutional Aviation Desk Maxim

web_blocks.html: Afcom Holdings Limited was formed in February 2013 in Chennai, Tamil Nadu [1, 2]. Captain Deepak Parasuraman, a career cargo pilot, co-founded the firm with Wing Commander Jaganmohan Manthena (Retd.), a former Indian Air Force officer [1, 6, 7]. For almost ten years, Afcom did not hold its own airline permit [4]. Instead, it worked as a light cargo broker [1, 4]. It booked belly space and third-party wet-leased freighters to fly airport-to-airport cargo between South India and Southeast Asia [1, 4]. Annual sales stayed below ₹15 crore through FY21 (₹13.89 crore revenue, -₹4.20 crore net loss) [17]. Then COVID-19 grounded passenger jets and created a sharp shortage of belly cargo space across the Bay of Bengal [17].

From FY22 to FY24, Afcom rode post-COVID supply-chain shifts and steady regional factory trade [17, 18]. Revenue rose from ₹48.27 crore in FY22 to ₹84.14 crore in FY23, then hit ₹148.19 crore in FY24 [17, 18]. Profits grew each year too, with PAT rising from ₹5.15 crore to ₹13.59 crore and ₹25.44 crore [17, 18]. Still, third-party wet-leases capped margins [4, 10]. In a wet-lease, the aircraft owner supplies the plane, crew, upkeep, and insurance (ACMI) [4, 10]. That model left Afcom dependent on outside carriers for schedules, route rights, and planes [4, 10]. To earn full cargo airline margins, Afcom needed its own DGCA Air Operator's Certificate (AOC) and dedicated dry-leased freighters [4, 7].

Two big steps in 2024 changed the business. First, in August 2024, Afcom ran its IPO on the BSE SME board (scrip code 544224) and raised about ₹74 crore [3, 18]. The cash paid for aircraft lease deposits, startup costs, and working capital [3, 18]. Second, in December 2024, the DGCA granted Afcom its formal AOC [4, 7]. That permit turned the charter broker into a scheduled Indian international cargo airline based at Chennai Airport [4, 7]. Management signed 96-month (eight-year) dry leases with Ireland's Spectre Air Capital for two 2000-vintage Boeing 737-800BCF freighters [4, 5]. These planes are registered as VT-AFO (MSN 28617, ex-Yakutia Airlines) and VT-AFC (MSN 30160, ex-Azur Air) [4, 5]. Afcom later added a third B737-800BCF to its fleet [8].

web_blocks.takeaway: Afcom's 2024–2026 leap was engineered by replacing high-cost wet-leases with long-term dry-leased B737-800BCFs and equity-funded lease deposits, while late-2026 brought subsidiary consolidation and a co-founder board exit.

web_blocks.html: By early 2026, Afcom won **Designated Indian Carrier** status under India's air treaties [9]. That status opened up statutory tax waivers, including Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) VAT relief at hubs like Tamil Nadu [9]. Red Sea shipping delays and airspace shifts also pushed urgent electronics, pharma, and factory goods onto air charters [1, 9]. As a result, FY26 revenue jumped 142% YoY to ₹583.00 crore (total income ₹587.73 crore), with ₹122.00 crore in PAT [1, 9, 10]. Next, Afcom laid plans to reach five narrowbodies and signed a Letter of Intent (LOI) for up to four Boeing 777-8F widebody jets [7, 10]. To fund that expansion, it ran a ₹199.84 crore QIP in May 2026 alongside a ₹104.47 crore share issue and 11.65 lakh warrants [7, 10, 12]. Those deals brought big institutions onto the register while cutting promoter stake from 42.73% at IPO to 35.40% by September 2026 [1, 19]. On November 12, 2026, co-founder Wing Commander Jaganmohan Manthena (Retd.) resigned as Non-Executive Non-Independent Director and stepped down from the Audit and Nomination & Remuneration Committees—two weeks after Afcom deferred a proposed 10.43 lakh share (3.61%) inter-se transfer from Manthena to promoter Manjula Annamalai due to statutory share lock-in [27, 29].

A key barrier protects Afcom's scheduled cargo AOC [4, 7]. Winning an international cargo AOC from the DGCA takes years of proof [4, 7]. A carrier must prove aircraft airworthiness, flight dispatch, pilot training, and safety systems—hurdles that block pure freight brokers [4, 7]. Once certified, Afcom could negotiate traffic rights directly with foreign aviation regulators across ASEAN and SAARC hubs [6, 21]. That turned its Chennai base into a dedicated narrowbody cargo hub rather than an ad-hoc charter desk [6, 21].

Afcom's jump from ₹13.89 crore revenue in FY21 to ₹583.00 crore in FY26 also highlights a key funding pattern [1, 17]. Every growth step—from the ₹74 crore August 2024 IPO to the ₹304 crore May 2026 QIP and share package—relied on fresh equity rather than internal cash [10, 12, 18]. By September 30, 2026, Afcom had deployed ₹95.63 crore of its ₹199.84 crore QIP proceeds (primarily ₹52.11 crore in aircraft lease deposits) and reported its first consolidated results incorporating two subsidiaries [27, 28]. Capital efficiency now defines the next stage [10, 12]. Bringing in Bandhan Mutual Fund, Abakkus, and Ashish Kacholia eased near-term cash pressure [12]. At the same time, it raised the bar on fleet returns, board governance after a co-founder exit, and working-capital discipline [12, 27]. Future aircraft additions will test whether operations can self-fund growth without further dilution [10, 12]. Strong unit profits alone are not enough if lease deposits keep draining cash [10, 15].

web_blocks.title: Why the Wet-to-Dry Pivot Matters
paragraphs: In a wet-lease, an airline pays an hourly ACMI fee that includes the lessor's crew, upkeep margin, and risk fee [4, 10]. Shifting to 96-month dry leases brings pilots, dispatch, and maintenance in-house under Afcom's own DGCA AOC [4, 9]. When fleet use tops 80%, fixed costs drive 40% EBITDA margins, though rigid Ind AS 116 lease debt (~₹338 crore) hurts if cargo demand drops [4, 9, 10].

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand Afcom Holdings without getting swept up in headline growth percentages, you and I have to start in 2013—not 2026. For its first decade, Afcom was not an airline in the way most investors picture one. Founded in Chennai by Captain Deepak Parasuraman, a career cargo pilot, and co-promoter Wing Commander Jaganmohan Manthena (who later stepped down from the Board and its Audit Committee in November 2026 following a deferred inter-se promoter share transfer), the company spent years as an asset-light air freight aggregator. It bought space on other operators' aircraft and sold airport-to-airport capacity to freight forwarders across South and Southeast Asia.

That long apprenticeship matters for two reasons. First, it meant the founders learned where cargo actually flows—which corridors have two-way industrial demand, which forwarders pay on time, and which routes bleed cash on empty return legs—long before they signed an eight-year aircraft lease. Second, it explains why the financial statements before FY25 look nothing like the company operating today. In FY21, Afcom booked just ₹13.89 crore of revenue and posted a ₹4.20 crore net loss. By FY24, riding post-pandemic belly-space shortages, revenue had climbed to ₹148.19 crore and net profit to ₹25.44 crore, yet the business was still structurally capped by third-party wet-lease costs.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Every successful regional freighter story begins with an unglamorous brokerage phase. Learning the freight-forwarding trade on someone else's metal is cheap tuition; signing eight-year dry leases before you have proved route density is how airlines go broke.

book_subsections.title: The 2024–2026 Structural Breakpoint
paragraphs: Everything changed in a four-month window between August and December 2024. The August 2024 BSE SME IPO raised roughly ₹74 crore, giving Afcom the balance-sheet credibility to post aircraft security deposits. In December 2024, the DGCA awarded Afcom its formal Air Operator's Certificate. Suddenly, Afcom was no longer a tenant paying retail wet-lease rates; it was a scheduled Indian cargo carrier operating its own dry-leased Boeing 737-800BCFs out of Chennai.

When you strip away the jargon, dry-leasing two 2000-vintage converted 737s from Spectre Air Capital—and subsequently adding a third—did two things simultaneously. It cut unit operating costs per block hour, and once Afcom gained Designated Indian Carrier status in early 2026, it gained ATF VAT exemptions in hubs like Tamil Nadu. Combined with strong charter demand during regional maritime and airspace disruptions, revenue more than doubled in FY26 to ₹583 crore while operating margins jumped to 40%. Yet that speed came at a capital cost: heavy lease deposits and induction outlays forced Afcom back to the equity markets in May 2026 for nearly ₹200 crore via QIP (of which ₹95.63 crore was deployed by September 2026) and over ₹104 crore via preferential shares, diluting promoter ownership from 42.73% down to 35.40% even before co-founder Jaganmohan Manthena's November 2026 board exit.

book_subsections.title: Why Vintage Freighters and Eight-Year Leases Cut Both Ways
paragraphs: There is one more detail from the 2024–2025 fleet induction that you should keep in your mental notebook. The first two aircraft Afcom dry-leased—VT-AFO and VT-AFC—are 2000-vintage Boeing 737-800 passenger airframes converted into freighters. In air cargo, flying older converted airframes is standard practice because freighters fly far fewer daily cycles than passenger jets, keeping capital costs low. However, eight-year dry leases mean Afcom also carries the heavy maintenance reserves and C-check obligations over the lease term.

As long as utilization stays above 80% and regional charter yields remain firm, those fixed lease commitments act like rocket fuel for operating margins. If regional freight rates ever normalize or an aircraft sits grounded for unscheduled maintenance, those same fixed commitments turn into a relentless cash drain. That is the core cyclical tension we will trace through every chapter of this dossier.

book_subsections.title: Why the DGCA Air Operator's Certificate Changed Everything
paragraphs: Think about what separates a freight broker from a certified airline. Before December 2024, Afcom had to rent aircraft with another operator's crew, insurance, and maintenance wrapped inside an all-in hourly wet-lease rate. Whenever passenger demand surged or an external lessor reassigned an airframe, Afcom's schedule flexibility vanished and its gross margin was capped by the lessor's markup.

Winning the DGCA Air Operator's Certificate flipped that relationship overnight. With its own AOC, Afcom could lease bare metal—dry-leasing two 2000-vintage Boeing 737-800BCFs from Spectre Air Capital on 96-month terms and later adding a third aircraft—while hiring its own pilots, engineers, and dispatchers. That shift gave management control over flight schedules, bilateral route rights across Southeast Asia, and, critically, eligibility for Designated Indian Carrier tax exemptions on jet fuel.

Of course, dry-leasing cuts both ways. Eight-year lease commitments turn variable broker costs into fixed monthly obligations, which is why Afcom had to raise roughly ₹74 crore in its August 2024 BSE SME IPO and another ₹304 crore across its May 2026 QIP and preferential issue to fund security deposits and entry-into-service expenses.

book_subsections.title: The Capital-Raise Cadence Behind the Fleet Ramp
paragraphs: When you trace Afcom's corporate history from 2013 through 2026, a clear pattern stands out: every major operational leap was funded by an external capital raise. The ₹74 crore BSE SME IPO in August 2024 paid for the initial aircraft lease deposits and entry-into-service costs required to activate the December 2024 DGCA Air Operator's Certificate. Less than two years later, the May 2026 QIP of ₹199.84 crore and preferential issue of ₹104.47 crore funded the next wave of fleet deposits and working capital.

There is nothing inherently wrong with raising growth equity to build an airline—in fact, it is far safer than loading up on short-term bank debt. However, it means future returns on capital depend on whether those newly inducted airframes can self-fund the next aircraft without tapping shareholders for a third time.

For investors studying Indian aviation, that transition from an asset-light charter broker in FY21 to a scheduled international cargo airline in FY25 and FY26 is rare. Most startups fail before securing a DGCA Air Operator's Certificate or institutional QIP backing. Afcom cleared both hurdles, which is why its operational execution commands respect even as its balance sheet demands scrutiny.

Notice also how the May 2026 QIP changed the conversation around governance. Bringing in marquee domestic mutual funds and seasoned institutional investors imposed a new level of quarterly scrutiny on fleet deployment, receivable collections, and capital allocation discipline.

Keep that capital-raise cadence in mind as we move into Chapter 2 to examine what Afcom actually flies, which routes carry the highest yields, and how its GSSA network fills the belly of its three narrowbodies.
